title: Passive quantum memory
why: Gemini 4 Argon does most of the math for Stanford physicist Patrick Hayden, showing that a quantum memory can keep its data safe on its own, with no constant fixing, even when warm and jostled, a question open since Alexei Kitaev's early work on quantum computers.

title: Diffie–Hellman problem
why: Working with Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Opus 5.5, Yuwen Zhou drops a condition from Ueli Maurer's 30-year-old result, showing that breaking a basic way computers agree on secret keys is as hard as the math problem behind it, given a short hint.

title: Non-overlapping codes
why: Simon Blackburn proves the most code words possible when no word's ending can match the start of any word, beating Vladimir Levenshtein's 1970 limit, with GPT-6 Astra writing one of the paper's key proofs.

title: Frostbite
why: Architect Labs' AI agents design a new computer processor on their own, from its basic commands to the chip layout; in simulation it does 4.59 times as much work per watt as a comparable modern design.

title: Smoktunowicz's gap theorem
why: Working alone for 94 minutes, GPT-6.2 Astra writes the first computer-checked proof of a 2006 theorem by mathematician Agata Smoktunowicz about how fast certain kinds of algebra can grow, taking its own route rather than hers.

title: El-Zahar–Erdős conjecture
why: Chenghua Liu and Boning Meng, working with GPT-6, answer a 1985 question of Mohamed El-Zahar and Paul Erdős with a no: networks that need many colors so linked dots differ, yet never split into two unlinked parts that each need many.

title: Stafford's conjecture
why: AI agents write the first full proof of Toby Stafford's 1978 claim about an algebra used in quantum physics and have a computer check every step, for Christopher Albert, Johanna Moser and Maximilian Philipp.

title: McKay–Praeger conjecture
why: Ning Su and Binzhou Xia, working with GPT-6, prove that almost every network where all points look alike is built from a set of symmetries, as Brendan McKay and Cheryl Praeger predicted.

title: Sample compression
why: Google's Cogentic agents running Gemini 4 Carbon prove on their own that anything a machine can learn can be captured in a handful of examples, about the square of the task's difficulty, the first such limit for a question Sally Floyd and Manfred Warmuth posed in 1995.

title: Additive squares
why: GPT-6 writes almost all of a paper for Jeffrey Shallit that solves a problem open over 50 years: an endless string of just six numbers where no two side-by-side stretches share both length and total, checked by computer.

title: Bounded integer programming
why: Given two earlier papers by Lin Chen, Yuchen Mao and Guochuan Zhang, GPT-6 finds a faster way than theirs to pick the best whole numbers within limits, a basic planning problem, with almost no human help.

title: QMA and QCMA
why: With GPT-6 Astra writing nearly the entire proof, Yiming Wang shows a case where evidence held in a quantum computer can convince a checker of things that no amount of ordinary written evidence can.

title: Cubic Schrödinger equation
why: Xi Chen, working with ChatGPT 6, builds waves on a square with wrap-around edges whose energy keeps moving into ever smaller ripples without end, answering a question of Jean Bourgain.

title: nginx2root
why: With no human guidance, Xint's AI finds four flaws that let attackers take over servers running nginx, the software behind about a third of websites; a Xint researcher found a fifth, hidden since 2015.

title: GPU chip design
why: OpenAI's models redesign parts of AMD's top graphics chip for up to 14% better speed, power use and size, about a year of engineering in under five months; AMD puts some of the changes in a chip it has sent to be made.

title: Topological overlap
why: Directed by Sergey Norin, GPT-6 Astra proves exactly how crowded some point must get when a triangle-like shape from higher dimensions is squashed into fewer, confirming a conjecture of Boris Bukh, Jiří Matoušek and Gabriel Nivasch.

title: Shortest paths on 4-polytopes
why: Working with ChatGPT, Igor Pak proves that finding the shortest route across the surface of a four-dimensional solid is as hard as the toughest puzzles computers face, disproving several conjectures along the way.

title: Positroid conjecture
why: ChatGPT-6 Astra proves a conjecture of Luis Ferroni, Katharina Jochemko and Benjamin Schröter about counting grid points inside certain shapes, in a 117-page proof that Ferroni only steered.

title: Navier–Stokes blowup
why: Working with Claude, Tristan Buckmaster and Levent Alpöge prove that the equations of fluid flow can break down even when nothing stirs the fluid, the version of the $1 million prize problem experts wanted.

title: Euler blowup
why: With AI help, Levent Alpöge, Tristan Buckmaster and Matei Coiculescu prove that a frictionless fluid in a box with wrap-around sides can suddenly spin infinitely fast at one point, with every step checked by computer.

title: McEliece challenges
why: MiniMax's unreleased model cracks the secret keys in 55 unsolved challenges for McEliece, an encryption method built to resist quantum computers, then breaks several dropped candidates for US encryption standards in practice for the first time.

title: Metal–organic frameworks
why: AI agents built by Théo Jaffrelot Inizan, Kristin Persson and Omar Yaghi design new sponge-like crystals that soak up carbon dioxide and pull water out of the air; chemists make four of them in the lab.

title: MONAI Label zero-day
why: AI agents run by China-linked hackers find an unknown flaw in MONAI Label, software for labeling medical scans, then use it to take over a university server with little human help.

title: Masullo's GRH proof
why: AI models help mathematicians find problems within hours in Alessandro Masullo's human-written attempt at a broader version of the Riemann hypothesis, posted by Ravi Vakil.

title: Valiant's conjecture
why: An internal Claude model proves that VP and VNP are different, settling Leslie Valiant's 1979 conjecture, the algebraic version of P versus NP; hours later OpenAI posts a proof of its own.

title: Auction pricing limits
why: Gemini 4 proves that fixed price tags set before buyers arrive one by one can come close to the best possible sale but never within a constant factor of it, answering a question open since 2015.

title: Smale's ninth problem
why: An OpenAI model solves linear programs, the math behind scheduling and logistics, in strongly polynomial time to settle Stephen Smale's ninth problem from 1998; a companion paper shows that no pivot rule can make the simplex method run in polynomial time.

title: Hadwiger's covering conjecture in 3D
why: Working with Gemini 4 Carbon, Dror Aiger, Sariel Har-Peled and Goran Žužić prove Hugo Hadwiger's 1957 covering conjecture in three dimensions: every 3D convex body can be covered by eight smaller copies of itself.

title: Sunflower conjecture
why: An OpenAI model proves Paul Erdős and Richard Rado's 1960 sunflower conjecture for any fixed number of petals: a family of sets only has to be exponentially large in their size to contain a group that all share the same core.

title: Protein binders
why: GPT-6.2 designs the shapes of new proteins using only reasoning and code; 35 of the 322 that Onava makes in the lab bind their targets, including PD-L1, which some cancers use to hide from the immune system.

title: 1808 fur-trade sketchbook
why: In 22 minutes, GPT-6.2 Astra identifies French aristocrat Louis-Guy-Charles-Guillaume de Rohan-Chabot as the artist of an anonymous 1808 fur-trade sketchbook at Yale for historian Mark Humphries, then finds his overlooked journal in Cleveland, which records drawing one of its views.

title: Integer factoring
why: Gemini 4 proves that whole numbers can be factored in the same running-time class as the 1990 number field sieve without the unproven assumptions it rests on, with a companion paper giving the first method without randomness that beats exponential time.

title: Discrete logarithms
why: Gemini 4 finds a way to compute discrete logarithms in finite fields of small characteristic faster than quasi-polynomial time, beating the bound that has stood since 2014 on a core problem behind cryptography.

title: Log-rank conjecture
why: Gemini 4 breaks the square-root barrier for László Lovász and Michael Saks's 1988 log-rank conjecture, improving on Shachar Lovett's 2014 bound for how much two computers must communicate.

title: Edge reconstruction conjecture
why: Gemini 4 proves Frank Harary's 1964 edge reconstruction conjecture, that a network can be rebuilt from copies of it each missing one link, for every network with at least 1,000 times as many links as points.

title: Approximate Nash equilibria
why: Gemini 4 finds a polynomial-time algorithm for 1/5-approximate Nash equilibria in two-player games, beating the one-third barrier that stood for nearly 20 years.
